Injecting the surface-toggle device into prism-codex.html, the CSS I added contained .pfx-surf{ and I located the HTML insertion point with indexOf(pfx-surf) - which matched inside the stylesheet in the head, long before any lead paragraph. lastIndexOf then returned -1, and h.slice(0,-1) is the ENTIRE document, so the tail got appended twice: 2.67 MB, leads 1-9 repeating as 11-19. Caught by COUNTING leads, not by reading the page - a 1.4 MB file looks fine at both ends. Reverted with git checkout and rebuilt behind three refuse-to-write assertions (lead count unchanged, final size == predicted +/-4 bytes, id=pfxSurf present exactly once); result 1,430,086 bytes against 1,430,086 predicted, exact. GENERALISES: never search a document for a token you also just wrote into that document, and never trust a -1 index into a slice. Workgraph N29.
src: prism codex surface device, 2026-09-15; workgraph N29

detail: 2026-09-15. Evidence-gated state transitions: --advance is its own verb taking {target, state, evidence}, where evidence must carry a checkable anchor (a commit sha, an artifact version vN, or a passing *_OK verify token) and a bare assertion is refused, never defaulted. Five refuse-to-write gates run on every call including --dry: node count and ids unchanged, edges byte-identical, exactly the named targets changed, only state/priorState/advanced moved on them, and the rest of the file untouched outside this pass. Atomic - one refused advance and nothing is written. Also adds a validated group field on corrections, which fixes the class of node written without a lane and therefore stored but unrenderable, since every renderer filters on group alone. Closes workgraph N28.

2026-09-15. D1, D2 and D3 filed as this-stage decision nodes; B2 advanced to corrected-verified, B18 to design-decision-locked and B27 to done, each on a checked anchor rather than an assertion. Graph at 78 nodes / 84 edges with three-copy parity across the mirror, the rendered codex and the canonical copy tracked in Prism, proven by VERIFY_WORKGRAPH_OK rather than by eyeballing the page.

2026-09-15. Closes B27s last named gap. 1,751,772 bytes, zero placeholders, three real embeds - the gap B27 had been carrying was a codex that named surfaces it never showed, so the close is measured on real embedded content rather than on the page existing.

The skill was a LIVE HOME WITH NO SOURCE BEHIND IT: ~/.claude/skills/griot-gold-log held only scripts/, with no SKILL.md and no directory at all in digital-griot-skills - an ungated propagation target in the sense of invariant I11, where the only copy that existed was the one nothing could refresh it from. item: DEFECT FOUND, FIXED AND RE-PROVEN: --renderer shell drew lanes and never reached Shell.tsx
detail: Asking the engine for a UI design at hi fidelity returned a re-skinned archify lane diagram. The emitter's own docblock (emit-screen.mjs:307) said the shell renderer drew the same lane-band shape as the document path - so --renderer shell had never emitted UI chrome, it emitted the lane diagram under a different flag. Fingerprints proved it: shell-mid and nodegraph-mid both hashed b90fd90fa9c69bee at 194 elements, the same drawing. Shell.tsx (13,207 b) was never reached and 'fidelity' had zero occurrences in engine src. This is B7 and the fidelity half of B17, measured rather than claimed. RE-MEASURED THE SAME DAY by running the engine's own comparator: six artifacts, six distinct fingerprints (shell 149/255/316 el, nodegraph 126/186/280 el), verdict PASS with 0 structurally-identical pairs. 'fidelity' now occurs 29x in src via core/fidelity.ts, and 04-shell/chrome.ts lifts the real Shell.tsx chrome behind a drift GATE (check-chrome-drift.mjs, exit 0, 45 spec'd classes) that goes red if a class is renamed - the hard form, not a keep-in-sync note. Caveat kept rather than glossed: the Prism-side fix is still UNCOMMITTED, so no sha anchors it and B7/B17 were deliberately not advanced.

item: DEFECT: the panel-system run printed DONE_PANEL_SYSTEM with three of its own criteria unmet
detail: The run wrote its terminal heartbeat and exited reporting success while three contract requirements had not happened: the promote rule was not built, references/panel-system.md was not written, and the transient API was not reachable from the page. The third is the sealed-IIFE defect above - meaning the run reported a panel system DONE while nothing on the page could open a panel. This is precisely the failure the invariants exist for: a completion claim carrying no evidence from the run that made it. Filed against the RUN, not the work - the code that landed was sound, the claim about it was not. Re-measured 2026-09-16: the promote rule is now built (helper.js:1079, :1728, :1779-1795) and the API is now reachable (:2007), but references/panel-system.md is STILL ABSENT, so this stays open on one gap.

Directly relevant to Anansi: if motion is generated from primitives at runtime rather than authored as clips, the Trigger-Condition-Instruction model gets a generative animation layer under it. Slug points at the public mirror of the NVIDIA release. · also R3F Studio, AUXGOD.

Community C++/GGML port of MotionBricks that dynamically generates animation from keyframes on low-VRAM GPUs or pure CPU, plugged into Unreal through MCP. Same lesson as kimodo.cpp and worth pairing with it: the GGML conversion is what makes a real-time motion model usable inside an engine on a laptop. · also R3F Studio, The Griot Model.

A learned compact representation for unified autoregressive rigging - predicts a skeleton and weight distribution straight from a mesh, and drove the ComfyUI workflow that auto-rigged a generated character with a UE5 skeleton. This is the missing automation in R3F Studio's CC5-to-Blender path: rigging without a manual weight-paint pass. · also GBFolio, Anansi.

C++/GGML conversion of VAST-AI's SkinTokens that auto-rigs a mesh ready for animation without a CUDA stack - the third of the localai-org ports (with kimodo.cpp and motion-bricks.cpp) that together form a CPU-runnable rig-and-animate chain. Worth treating as one shelf cluster rather than three unrelated repos. · also GBFolio, The Griot Model.

Tencent's open image-to-3D generator, with a smart-topology mode for low-poly meshes and (per the pipeline videos) the useful property of returning models in their original position so multi-part characters reassemble. The free, self-hostable half of the generation step that Tripo charges for. · also Lucid, Anansi.

Tencent's hosted product layer over the Hunyuan3D models, named as a high-quality option for the retopology step specifically. The models are open (Hunyuan3D-2.1) but the Studio app is a closed hosted service - land it as a service to evaluate, not code to lift. · also Lucid.

Commercial image/text-to-3D service whose P2 model is rated the best auto-topology in this batch - low-poly quads directly, no manual retopo. Closed paid product with no public repo; VAST AI's open TripoSR/TripoSG line is the research it descends from. Honest read: the quality bar R3F Studio's open pipeline is measured against. · also Lucid, Anansi.

Deemos' image-to-editable-3D-world tool: part extraction into real meshes, scene placement, a 3D Gaussian Splat background and export to Blender and Unreal. Closed commercial product - but the architecture (meshes for the things you touch, splats for everything else) is the single most transferable idea here for GBFolio's environment story. Also named separately in the news roundup as the Hyper3D world generator. · also R3F Studio, Lucid.

World Labs' next-generation world model, stitching one or more images into a navigable 3D world; waitlist-only with no code or repo. Tracked as a watch item: if navigable-world generation becomes reachable, GBFolio's portfolio environment and Lucid's scene output both change shape. · also Lucid, R3F Studio.

Microsoft research model that recalculates scans, reconstructions and AI meshes into editable quad topology, with code reportedly released. The ASR renders the name as 'Squad Gen' and no repo resolved on a direct GitHub probe - slug unverified, needs a manual pass before it can be adopted. If real, it is the open answer to Tripo P2's retopology. · also Anansi.

Free webcam face-capture tool recording ARKit-style shape keys and head motion as a track for game engines. No repo resolved on a direct probe - slug unverified. Relevant as the cheap facial-performance input for GBFolio's avatar work and for anything Ashe drives with a talking head. · also R3F Studio, Ashe.

Exoside's paid local Blender add-on for auto-retopology, recommended in the fully-local character build as the better option over free remeshers at a $19 perpetual price. Closed commercial add-on, no repo - a cheap dependency for the R3F Studio pipeline rather than something to build. · also GBFolio.

Commercial baking and look-dev tool with a proper cage, described as easier for beginners than Blender's baker. Closed product, no repo. Named here because the baking step is where the AI-generated-asset pipeline most often breaks - worth knowing the escape hatch exists. · also GBFolio.

Adobe's free hosted auto-rigger and animation library, used here only as a source of an exported T-pose skeleton for the humanoid half of a hybrid creature. Closed service with no repo, and a long-term risk as a pipeline dependency - which is exactly why SkinTokens and AccuRig matter. · also R3F Studio, Anansi.

Reallusion's free local marker-based auto-rigger: rigs an FBX character in about a minute and exports in T-pose, and worked even on the upper body of a non-humanoid. Free but closed, no repo. It already sits in R3F Studio's Reallusion lineage (CC5/iClone8), so it is the incumbent the open SkinTokens route has to beat. · also GBFolio, Anansi.

iClone's lip-sync feature, applied to imported ElevenLabs audio to drive a character's mouth. Closed Reallusion feature, no repo. The suite-relevant piece is the shape of the step - audio in, viseme track out - which is the contract any open replacement in the R3F/GBFolio avatar path has to meet. · also GBFolio, Ashe.

Reallusion's real-time animation app where the scene, lights, camera moves and final render were built before any AI pass. Closed commercial product. It is already one end of R3F Studio's declared pipeline (CC5/iClone8 into Blender into the ecosystem), so this batch is direct evidence about the tool the pipeline starts in. · also GBFolio, Ashe.

New iClone workspace that turns a viewport capture into AI-styled image and video output - a render alternative that swaps the render farm for a diffusion pass. Closed feature, no repo. This is exactly the 3D-to-styled-output adapter Lucid is supposed to own, demonstrated inside someone else's app. · also Ashe, R3F Studio.

Reallusion's character authoring app, used to build the character before importing into iClone. Closed commercial product. Named in the suite context already (the CC5 half of the CC5/iClone8-to-Blender path) - this batch confirms the workflow is still the working route for a production-grade rigged human. · also R3F Studio, Anansi.

Character Creator plugin that builds a custom head from reference. Closed Reallusion plugin, no repo. The photo-to-head step in the avatar pipeline - worth naming because it is the piece most likely to be replaced by an open image-to-3D model in the next year. · also R3F Studio.

iClone's PopcornFX-based particle plugin, used for the green particle effect in the making-of. Closed plugin, no repo. Tracked as the VFX/particle layer of the real-time animation stack - the thing Lucid and Ashe both eventually need an answer for. · also Ashe, R3F Studio.

Hosted hub that chains prop extraction, multiview, Tripo generation, retopology and some texturing in one place, with free credits on signup. Closed product, no repo. Its real value as a reference is the chaining: it is a worked example of the multi-stage 3D pipeline UI that Lucid is meant to be for the suite. · also R3F Studio.

Free AI texturing tool that respects the baked normal map, with projection and patch brushes for inpainting broken texture regions and full re-projection as layers. Named in two separate pipelines as the fix for AI-generated texture damage. No repo resolved - free but closed. The 'respects the normal map' behaviour is the requirement, whoever supplies it. · also Lucid, GBFolio.

Creature-rigging service with template skeletons (a spider template here) plus ready idle, walk and attack animations - the non-humanoid answer to Mixamo. Closed hosted service, no repo. Relevant to Anansi precisely because non-humanoid rigs are where every automatic pipeline in this batch fell over. · also R3F Studio, AUXGOD.

Alternative creature-rigging tool named as a community favourite alongside Animate Anything. Closed service, no repo resolved. Parked undecided next to its sibling - two services solving the same non-humanoid rig gap is a signal that the gap is real and open code will follow. · also R3F Studio.

Unreal marketplace add-ons for sky, weather and mood that the creator says he uses constantly. Closed paid assets, no repo. Named because it points at a real gap: an agent-native engine needs a first-class environment/time-of-day system, not a per-scene hand-build. · also GBFolio, R3F Studio.

The second image-to-3D generator now shipping natively in ComfyUI alongside Trellis 2, said to give slightly more shape accuracy and to be strong on hats and hard-surface parts. The name is badly ASR-garbled across two videos (PixArt-alpha, Pixel 3D, PixArt 3D, Pixologic 3D) and no repo resolved on a direct probe - slug unverified, needs a manual identification pass. · also Lucid.

Browser-based, frame-exact animation review player built by animators: versioning, animator-specific statuses, drawing tools, range comments and live collaborative sessions. Proprietary, currently free beta. The review-and-annotate layer is a direct model for Ashe (shot review) and for Kweli's comprehension-before-commitment approval loop. · also Kweli, Lucid.

Used across this batch as the local agent for brainstorming, reference prep, and the procedural/IK leg animation work in Unity and Unreal - i.e. as a 3D-pipeline participant, not just a code tool. Worth landing on the shelf in its own right because it is the runtime the whole Griot plugin/skill layer targets. · also Djeli, R3F Studio, Anansi.

Free (account-gated) Blender extension exposing Blender tools plus 3D, image and video generation APIs to any agent, with an in-viewport chat. Closed product, no repo. The pattern to steal is the bundling: one MCP surface that gives the agent both the DCC's operations and the generation APIs, rather than making it juggle two servers. · also Lucid, Djeli.

Open MCP server that lets an agent drive, run and test a Unity project - not just edit files but execute the loop. The run-and-test half is the part Anansi needs: an agent-native engine is only agent-native if the agent can also observe the result of what it built. · also Prism, R3F Studio.

Unreal Engine agent tooling paired with UE 5.8's own native MCP - free with registration, and the most mature engine-side agent bridge in this batch. Reference implementation for how an engine bridge splits work between the engine's native MCP and a community layer on top. · also R3F Studio, Prism.

MCP server fronting fal.ai - the broadest model coverage in the batch (sound, music, video, 3D) with the caveat that you must pick the model by hand. That caveat is the product gap Lucid is for: one surface that routes to the right generator instead of making you name it. · also Ashe, Sigil.

MCP server that hands an agent Figma design context - used here to export Figma images as oriented planes into Blender, which is a design-to-3D bridge nobody planned for. Relevant to Lucid and Sigil as the design-source adapter, and to Djeli as a panel that makes design context first-class. · also Sigil, Djeli.

Prime Intellect's evaluation package - the speaker's claim is that it reproduces every eval shown in the talk, which is the whole point: a harness without reproducible evals is an anecdote. This is the missing gate under prism-eval's version comparisons. · also Valence, Kente.

Stanford project running the entire personal AI stack - inference, agents, memory, learning - on device, with llama.cpp/Ollama/vLLM/SGLang listed as interchangeable inference primitives. No repo resolved on a direct probe: slug unverified. It is the closest published statement of the thesis The Griot Model is arguing, so it deserves a manual identification pass. · also Kaleidoscope, Meridian.

YC's own open-source agent harness for work, used daily through Slack and a web UI. Described as open source in the talk but no repo resolved on a direct probe (the name is a two-letter token the ASR may have mangled) - slug unverified. The interesting part for Griot Hub is the surface choice: the harness lives where the work already happens, not in a dedicated app. · also Prism, Valence.

Optimises a system prompt by genetic search over candidate prompts rather than backpropagation - prompts as a trainable artifact. Directly relevant to Prism's skill layer: if a skill's instructions are searchable rather than hand-tuned, prism-eval stops being a vibe check. · also Kente, SkillForge.

The agent-orchestrator platform that built four games end to end in loop mode in this video - the creator's assessment of where it genuinely works and where it fails is the useful content. The name is heavily ASR-garbled (Tisana, the Sun, to sauna) and was not captured in the digest's own OSS list; no repo resolved - slug unverified. Landed anyway so the loop-mode orchestration lesson is not lost. · also Anansi, Djeli.

Geoffrey Litt's live-programming tool showing recorded return values and object state beside Ruby code - eight years on, still the cleanest demo of 'the program's actual behaviour, rendered in the margin'. Described as source available but no repo resolved on a probe: slug unverified. The margin-as-evidence-surface idea is the one Kaleidoscope and Valence keep reaching for. · also Valence, Djeli.

The Ruby interpreter's hook API for method call/return events - the single primitive that made Margin Notes trivial to build. The lesson is the leverage: one runtime hook turned an ambitious tool into a weekend. Worth asking what the equivalent single hook is for agent runs in Valence. · also Kaleidoscope, Prism.

Ink & Switch's dynamic-document prototype: an outliner where mentions, formulas and map/table/calendar views all sit over the same content. No public repo resolved - research prototype, slug unverified. This is Synaptiq's thesis stated by someone else: one substrate, many views, with agents as just another reader. · also Kaleidoscope, Meridian.

Research project whose rule is that all UI state must live in a multiplayer-synced database - no component-local state at all. No public repo resolved: slug unverified. A hard architectural constraint worth testing against Synaptiq's canvas, where agent writes and human edits have to converge on the same store anyway. · also Kaleidoscope, Griot Hub.

Shipped Notion primitive letting a coding agent embed arbitrary interactive HTML inside an editable document - the commercial proof that agent-authored interactive content inside a document is now table stakes. Closed product feature, no repo. Exactly the seam between Synaptiq's canvas and the artifact-style output the suite already produces. · also Kaleidoscope, Lucid.

Fuzzy string matching library whose README was a set of interactive explorations rather than prose - cited in the talk as the proof that documentation can be a thing you operate instead of a thing you read. That is the visual-first contract, shipped in a library README. · also Griot Viz Templates, Kaleidoscope.

Opinionated, AI-customisable Arch/Hyprland desktop setup - named independently in both catch-ups, once as a candidate for repurposing an idle PS4 into a Linux lab and once as an exemplar of malleable software. Relevant to Tesseract as the Hyprland-parity reference it is explicitly chasing on Windows. · also keylink, Personal.

Sandbox/dev-environment provider the guest builds in after prototyping a throwaway clone first - the workflow being: one disposable environment per experiment, kept isolated from the real machine. That is the missing boundary around Prism's autonomous runs and Spectrum's parallel stories. · also Djeli, Valence.

Blackmagic's free-tier NLE, used here to put a Blender playblast and the AI-generated video side by side for comparison. Closed product, no repo. Named because the A/B comparison step - render versus generation, same timeline - is a real workflow primitive Ashe should have rather than an afterthought. · also Lucid.

Open TensorRT feature that turns a Hugging Face checkpoint name into an optimised, deployable bundle in two commands, then runs inference - demoed across speech, reasoning, search, segmentation, depth, full-duplex voice and multi-GPU video on DGX Spark hardware. Covers both the Model Connect layer and the TensorRT compiler underneath it. The two-command checkpoint-to-deployable path is precisely the rung Kente's forge is trying to automate, and the cu128 Blackwell story matters directly on the ProArt's RTX 5060. · also Kente, Valence.

NVIDIA's open physics-aware world/video generation model family, used in the two-Spark multi-device demo. Open weights and open code, which makes it the rare world model the suite could actually run rather than watch - relevant to Lucid's video path and to Anansi if physics-aware generation ever meets the runtime. · also Lucid, Anansi.

NVIDIA's open full-duplex speech-to-speech model, demoed live - full duplex meaning it listens and speaks at once instead of taking turns. That is the exact property Audion's real-time listening and teleprompter overlay needs, and the open-weights version removes the API dependency from the critical path. · also The Griot Model, Damus, Kora.

The framework whose checkpoints Model Connect converts from, and the stated baseline every optimisation is measured against. Named here because it is the floor of Kente's forge and the reason the cu128 Blackwell wheel problem on the ProArt is a recurring tax rather than a one-off. · also The Griot Model, PlantID CNN.

Where Model Connect pulls weights from and where the ComfyUI workflows in the 3D batch fetch their clip-vision, diffusion and VAE safetensors - i.e. the single distribution point both halves of this catch-up depend on. Kente's ranked base-model and LoRA shortlists are, in practice, queries against this hub. · also The Griot Model, R3F Studio.

High-throughput serving engine listed as one of the interchangeable local inference primitives under Open Jarvis. The interchangeability claim is the useful part: if llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM and SGLang are swap-in equivalents behind one interface, The Griot Model's three-lane story needs exactly that interface. · also Kente, Valence.

Best overall output across thirteen Blender and game-dev tasks in the one-shot benchmark, but slowest and most expensive - the quality ceiling with a cost tail. Closed frontier model, no repo. Concrete evidence for Prism's Model Control Plane: the per-model ask/allow/deny policy exists because this trade-off is real and task-shaped. · also Djeli, R3F Studio.

Fastest and cheapest of the frontier models tested, with two outright failures across thirteen Blender and game-dev tasks. Closed model, no repo. The other end of the Model Control Plane trade-off - cheap enough to retry, unreliable enough that the retry has to be gated. · also Djeli.

Uneven performer in the same thirteen-task benchmark - strong on the Sekiro menu and off-road truck tests, weak elsewhere. Closed model, no repo. Useful as data rather than as a tool: task-shaped capability is the argument for per-task model selection rather than one default. · also Djeli.

Black Forest Labs' image model, used here to repose a generated character and split it into separable parts for per-part 3D generation. Open weights and open inference code. The part-separation trick is the pipeline unlock: it is what turns a single concept image into a multi-part 3D character. · also R3F Studio, Sigil.

The LoRA whose 'separate X onto a white background' keyword actually performs the character-into-parts split. Distributed as weights rather than a code repo and not resolved on a direct probe - slug unverified. A small, sharp example of the LoRA rung on Kente's customization ladder doing real pipeline work. · also Kente, R3F Studio.

Model used for the initial full-body character concept art before anything is generated in 3D. Closed hosted product, no repo. Named as the front of the concept-to-character pipeline - the step where art direction is still cheap to change. · also Sigil.

Google's image editing model, used across two pipelines to split concepts into building-block references, generate tileable textures, and derive additional PBR property maps from one well-structured colour map. Closed, no repo. That last trick - one colour map into a full material set - is a genuinely useful shortcut for the R3F Studio texture path. · also R3F Studio, Sigil.

The larger Nano Banana variant chosen for the 3D-to-image style pass in the iClone making-of - taking a rendered viewport and restyling it. Closed, no repo. Parked alongside its sibling; the 3D-capture-to-styled-image step is a Lucid adapter either way. · also Ashe, GBFolio.

The free surface used for the concept-splitting and tileable-texture generation in the all-free pipeline. Closed hosted product, no repo. Worth landing because the free tier is what makes the whole pirate-cave pipeline reproducible - a cost floor the suite's own adapters should respect. · also Sigil.

ByteDance's video model, used to turn a 3D viewport capture into a moving shot with camera motion applied - and, in three other videos in this batch, to upgrade a low-poly Blender playblast into a finished-looking shot. Closed, no repo. The playblast-as-video-reference workflow is the single most repeated technique across the whole 3D catch-up and belongs in Ashe. · also Lucid, GBFolio, AUXGOD.

Image generator used for reference art with a distinctive style that happened to fit one of the four games. Closed, no repo. Landed as one more generation adapter and as evidence for the routing argument: style fit, not benchmark score, is what decided which model got used. · also Sigil.

Meta's self-supervised vision backbone, required as one of the vision models the native ComfyUI image-to-3D workflows ask you to download. Open weights. Quietly the most load-bearing model in the 3D batch: the generators lean on its features rather than shipping their own encoder. · also Lucid, PlantID CNN.

The 40-layer vision model whose residual stream showed the high-activation artifact that register tokens were introduced to fix - the worked example in the ResNet-to-residual-stream history. Directly useful to Ophenia: it is a published case of a model's internal state carrying a readable artifact, which is what perceiving your own cognition would have to look like. · also Kente, PlantID CNN.

One-click portable ComfyUI installer for Windows, macOS and Linux with a dashboard for packages, environments and configuration - recommended over a manual setup by the creator who runs the whole local character pipeline. The install-and-environment problem is the real barrier to the local 3D lane on the ProArt; this is the shortest path past it. · also Lucid, Kente.

Text-to-speech source for the voice-over that then drove the lip-sync pass - closed service, but with an official open Python SDK (the slug) that is what an integration actually touches. The TTS-into-viseme chain is the same seam Audion, Ashe and GBFolio's talking avatar all need. · also Ashe, GBFolio, Lucid.

The video author's own Blender add-on that re-exports a collection and hot-reloads it in the browser on Shift+E - Blender-to-three.js hot reload in one keystroke. No repo resolved on a probe: slug unverified. This is the dev-loop ergonomics R3F Studio's Blender bridge is missing, described precisely enough to rebuild. · also GBFolio, Anansi.

Browser tool for inspecting an exported GLB - used here to catch a suspect material setup that would have shipped silently. The site itself is closed-source (its public repo is a feedback tracker, donmccurdy/glTF-Report-Feedback) and it runs on the open glTF-Transform engine, which is already on the shelf. A GLB lint pass belongs in R3F Studio's export gate. · also GBFolio, Anansi.

Scrapes each service's /metrics endpoint on a fixed interval and stores timestamped values in blocks - the pull-based collection model for 100+ microservices. Valence is Datadog-shaped for agents, and this is the reference architecture for the collection half: agents expose, the collector pulls, nobody writes a bespoke reporter. · also Meridian, Griot Hub.

Prometheus add-on - sidecar, store gateway and query components - that breaks the single-disk retention limit by sealing blocks to object storage and querying across them. This is the exact problem Valence hits the moment agent telemetry has to be retained longer than a laptop disk allows. · also Meridian, Kaleidoscope.

The dashboard layer, pointed at the federated query component rather than at any single collector - a deliberate decoupling so the dashboard never knows which store answered. Valence's UI should inherit that separation instead of binding panels to a specific backend. · also Meridian, Griot Hub.

The cluster hosting the 100+ microservices being scraped - present here as the environment that makes service discovery automatic rather than as a thing to adopt. Named so the shelf records the assumption: this architecture's ergonomics come from discovery, and a suite without an orchestrator has to supply that some other way. · also Prism.

Cheap, durable, effectively unlimited object storage for sealed metric blocks - the bottom tier that makes unbounded retention affordable. Closed commercial service, no repo; the interface is the point, and any S3-compatible store satisfies it. Landed as the storage assumption under the Thanos pattern. · also Meridian, Kaleidoscope.

Absorbs the huge write volume of viewing-history play/pause events at Netflix - the write-heavy leg of the polyglot-persistence example. Relevant to Valence and Meridian for the same reason: agent-step and attention events are high-volume appends, not transactions. · also Meridian, Synaptiq.

Powers search at Netflix because it is built to serve queries fast, sitting alongside three other stores rather than replacing them. The polyglot lesson lands directly on Kaleidoscope: the knowledge porter spans Claude memory, session JSONL, project docs and codebase docs, and pretending one store fits all of them is the mistake. · also Synaptiq, Cinopsis.

Netflix's memcached-based caching layer that makes the homepage - including continue-watching - load fast. The continue-watching shape is the interesting one for Griot Hub: a launcher's whole job is to answer 'where was I' instantly across every app, which is a cache problem before it is an orchestration problem. · also Meridian, Valence.

The core classical-ML library, cited in the feature-engineering primer as the thing that will not process null gaps - forcing an explicit imputation decision before training. The primer's thesis (a simple model with well-engineered features beats a deep net fed raw data) is the argument for Kente's lower rungs existing at all. · also PlantID CNN, Personal.

Git's native worktree feature - each branch gets its own working directory off one repo, which is the isolation primitive that lets several agents edit concurrently without colliding. Not a separate project (it ships inside git itself); the video's whole argument is that the capability is already there and only the CLI ergonomics are broken. · also Djeli, Prism Gavel.

The macOS/Linux package manager, cited as Worktrunk's primary install path (brew install worktrunk). Relevant to the suite only as a distribution channel - if Prism's CLI or a Fragment-scaffolded tool ever ships beyond winget, a tap is the expected front door. · also Fragment.

Rust's build tool and package manager; the second install lane for Worktrunk (cargo install worktrunk). Already the de-facto build surface for keylink's Tauri2/Rust stack, so it is infrastructure the suite is standing on rather than a candidate to adopt. · also Tesseract, Prism.

CLOSED commercial code-signing service (signpath.io, garbled as 'sin path io' in the ASR) - no public repo, so no slug. It grants free signing certificates to open-source projects, which is how Worktrunk ships a signed Windows binary. Directly relevant because Prism's NSIS installer and Tesseract's WinUI3 build both hit the unsigned-binary SmartScreen wall on Windows. · also Tesseract, keylink.

Audio-to-lead-sheet transcription model used by YuE2 to turn a source recording into an editable score before a cover is rendered; reported top on 10 of 13 benchmark metrics. NO standalone repo found for v2 - it is documented inside the YuE2 repo with weights on Hugging Face; v1 (SheetSage) is real and public at chrisdonahue/sheetsage. Slug left blank deliberately rather than guessed. · also Ashe, AUXGOD.

Music-understanding representation model used as SheetSage 2's encoder; reported top on 14 of 15 MARBLE metrics (garbled as 'Merit 2' in the ASR). NO public repo for v2 - weights on Hugging Face, documented in the YuE2 README; MERT v1 is real and public at yizhilll/MERT. Slug deliberately blank - unverified rather than invented. · also Kente, AUXGOD.

Evaluation benchmark and prompt set YuE2 reports its SongBench average against. NO separate repo found - it ships inside the YuE2 release, so no slug. Worth keeping for the evidence discipline it models: YuE2 states its cross-model margins are not statistically significant and only makes a confident claim where the ablation gap is real (0.647 vs 0.006 mAP on 948 works). · also Kente.

Plain-text music notation format (a community standard, not a repo) that YuE2 exports its melody-and-chord plan in. The pattern is the point for Kora: put a human-readable, agent-editable intermediate between the prompt and the render, so music generation becomes iterable instead of prompt-and-pray. Note YuE2 re-renders from the edited score - the original waveform is not preserved. · also Ashe, Lucid.

CLOSED commercial WordPress snippet manager (wpcodebox.com) - no public repo, so no slug. Its MCP server is what lets Claude Code write and activate PHP snippets on a live site, and it refuses to keep a snippet active once it errors. The safety pattern, not the product, is the takeaway: give the agent write access behind a guard that auto-disables broken code and hands the error back for repair. · also Kweli.

Open WordPress MCP stack from Soflyy giving agents shell, PHP eval, filesystem and process access - named in the video as the free alternative to WP CodeBox. Explicitly scoped to trusted dev environments only, which is the honest version of the permission boundary Prism keeps negotiating through its Model Control Plane. · also Kweli.

Long-running open WordPress breadcrumb plugin, deactivated live in the demo to prove an agent-written snippet was rendering the breadcrumbs itself. No suite fit on its own - parked as evidence for the video's real claim: a large share of installed plugins are small enough that an agent reproduces them on demand, moving the cost from vendor dependency to snippet maintenance. · also Realtor CMS.

CLOSED commercial WordPress page builder from Soflyy (breakdance.io) - no public repo, so no slug. It is in the harvest because it caused the demo's one real failure: the agent's page-duplication snippet copied the post but dropped Breakdance's design data from post meta, and even after the unslashing fix the CSS only reappeared after a re-save. The lesson generalises - agent-written code fails on the state nobody told it about. · also Realtor CMS.

The GPL CMS itself, plus the application-password mechanism that authenticates an MCP connection into a live site. Relevant to the dormant client lane as a base that already has a sanctioned agent write path, rather than something to build from scratch. · also Kweli, Mentorship Platform.

Python JIT that compiles numeric code to machine code via LLVM - and now, via QuantStack's port, runs entirely inside a browser notebook, with the demo showing roughly a 300x speedup on the math Python handles badly natively. The in-browser half is what matters: Kente's notebooks and the Math Formalism surface could ship compute to a tab instead of a backend. · also Math Formalism Ideation, PlantID CNN.

The compiler infrastructure under Numba's JIT - notable here because the entire LLVM-powered JIT was itself compiled to WebAssembly, which is the proof that binary-dependent stacks are now portable to a browser tab. Infrastructure to know about, not to adopt. · also Anansi.

The open-source group that ported Numba and its LLVM JIT to WebAssembly (garbled as 'Quatstack' in the ASR). An ORG, not a repo - no slug, deliberately. Worth tracking as the maintainers of the in-browser Jupyter/scientific-Python stack that a browser-side Kente notebook lane would sit on. · also Math Formalism Ideation.

The notebook environment where the in-browser Numba demo and its timings run, with Python itself executing locally rather than on a backend. Already the de-facto surface for Kente's forge and the Math Formalism thread; the Wasm story means that surface can now run client-side with a real JIT behind it. · also Math Formalism Ideation, PlantID CNN.

Browser-native sandbox from Leaning Technologies that runs Linux applications (Node, Rust, C++, Python preview) compiled to Wasm, with a persistent virtual filesystem, controlled networking, parallelism and multithreading - its makers call it an OS kernel for the web platform. Two claims worth testing: you target it directly instead of rewriting against WASI, and disk images stream block-by-block so only the parts of a stdlib you actually use get downloaded. That is a container-free execution lane for anything Djeli or Prism needs to run untrusted. · also Prism, Anansi, Kente.

The standard WebAssembly system interface for filesystem, clock and network syscalls outside the browser (garbled as 'WSI' and 'wazi' in the ASR). In the harvest as the baseline BrowserPod claims you can skip - if that claim holds, a Wasm execution lane costs no code changes; if it does not, WASI is the porting tax. · also Anansi.

Full Postgres compiled to WebAssembly - runs in a browser tab or embedded in Node.js, persists to local storage, and supports extensions including pgvector. This is the strongest single pull of the batch for the knowledge lane: Synaptiq, Kaleidoscope and Meridian all want a real relational-plus-vector store with zero server to run, and this is it. · also Kaleidoscope, Meridian, Djeli, Cinopsis.

Postgres extension for vector similarity search, and the reason PGlite is more than a toy: a local in-tab Postgres with pgvector makes low-profile semantic search viable with no vector-DB service at all. Graft's embeddings-first-class premise and Synaptiq's graph both land on this. · also Kaleidoscope, Hazine, Graft.

The language itself, cited as a first-class Wasm compile target and BrowserPod's first deployment priority - and already the implementation language of keylink and of Worktrunk. Listed for completeness rather than as a decision; it is a substrate the suite has chosen in places. · also Tesseract, Prism.

The container runtime, named in the InfoWorld piece only as the thing this whole approach deliberately avoids needing - the words Docker and containers never once came up. Parked as the baseline to measure against: if a Wasm lane can isolate agent output, the suite skips a container runtime it never wanted to wrangle. · also Djeli.
